questions.q: Why is the idempotency key stored with UNIQUE (user_id, idempotency_key) rather than unique on the key alone?
questions.explain: A key is chosen by the client. Scoping it per user means a guessed or colliding key never exposes another customer's stored result.
options: To save space in the index
Keys belong to one user: another user who sends the same key must not receive, or block, someone else's payment
Because keys are not random enough to be unique
Because PostgreSQL cannot index text alone

questions.q: The same Idempotency-Key arrives with a different card token. What does Oja answer, and why?
questions.explain: The stored SHA-256 fingerprint of the request is compared with the new one. Silently replaying would tell the client its new card was charged when it was not.
options: 201 with the stored payment, because the key matches
A new charge, because the request is different
422: a key belongs to one request; reusing it for another one is a client bug, and replaying the old result would lie about the new request

questions.q: What does CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_live_payment_per_order ON payments (order_id) WHERE status <> 'declined' guarantee?
questions.explain: A partial unique index only covers rows that match its WHERE. It stops two keys (two devices, an app bug) from charging one order twice, while still allowing retries after a decline.
options: An order has only one payment row ever
An order has at most one payment that is processing, unknown or succeeded; declined attempts do not count, so the customer can try another card
Two users cannot pay the same amount

questions.q: A client sends {"orderId": 7, "card": "tok_ok", "amountKobo": 100}. What amount is charged?
questions.explain: Prices and totals are facts the server owns. The schema only knows orderId and card, and the service copies the order's total into the payment row.
options: The order's total_kobo, loaded from the database; the schema strips amountKobo

questions.q: PayGate never answers the charge request, even after retries. Why does Oja record the payment as unknown instead of declined?
questions.explain: No answer is not a "no". The reconciliation job, or a client retry, asks the gateway later and settles the payment with the real outcome.
options: Because declined payments need a reason
The card may have been charged; calling it failed invites the customer to pay again and be charged twice

questions.q: Which status does POST /v1/payments return for a payment that is unknown?
questions.explain: 202 is honest: accepted, not finished. The client shows "payment pending" and polls GET /v1/payments/:id, or retries with the same key, which checks with the gateway.
options: 202 Accepted: the request was taken, the outcome is not known yet, and the client should check again later

questions.q: The HttpClient retries only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS by default. Why is it safe for the PayGate adapter to retry POST?
questions.explain: Retrying a non-idempotent request is how double charges happen. The key turns the POST into an idempotent operation at the gateway; without it the retry option would be a bug.
options: Every charge carries an Idempotency-Key that PayGate honours, so a repeated POST returns the first result instead of charging again
Because the POST body is small

questions.q: The adapter's key is oja-pay-<payment id>, not the client's key and not a new random value per attempt. Why?
questions.explain: A new key per attempt would let each attempt charge. Deriving it from our own payment id ties the key to the thing that must be charged once.
options: Every attempt to charge that one payment, including a retry hours later by reconciliation or a client retry, must reach the gateway with the same key
To hide the client's key from logs

questions.q: Why does the service call the gateway between two transactions instead of inside one?
questions.explain: Transaction 1 records the intent ("processing"), the call happens, transaction 2 records the outcome. If we crash in between, the "processing" row tells reconciliation what to look up.
options: A transaction open during a slow network call holds locks for as long as the gateway takes, and a rollback cannot undo a charge anyway

questions.q: settle runs UPDATE payments SET status = $2 … WHERE id = $1 AND status IN ('processing', 'unknown'). What happens when the reconciler settles a payment a client retry has already settled?
questions.explain: Making the state change conditional on the current state makes it idempotent. Several paths may report an outcome; only the first one counts.
options: The status is overwritten and a second event is written
The UPDATE matches no row, so nothing changes and no second outbox event is written
The order is marked paid twice

questions.q: Why is payment.succeeded written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the status, instead of being published directly?
questions.explain: Publishing before the commit can announce something that is then rolled back; publishing after it can be lost in a crash. The outbox row commits atomically with the change, and a relay publishes it.
options: Because the event bus is slow
The event then exists if and only if the status change committed: no event for a rolled-back change, and no lost event if we crash right after committing
Because events must be stored forever

questions.q: The relay publishes an event and then marks the row published. What happens if it crashes between the two steps?
questions.explain: There is no way to make "publish" and "mark" one atomic step across two systems. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers is the standard answer.
options: The event is published again on the next sweep; delivery is at least once, so consumers must be idempotent
The database rolls back the publish

questions.q: Which layer stops a duplicate SMS when the worker sent it and then crashed before writing the notifications row?
questions.explain: The queue and the table only know what was recorded. Between sending and recording, only the receiving side can recognise the repeat, which is why the key travels with the message.
options: The key passed to the SMS provider, which lets the provider drop a message it has already delivered

questions.q: Reconciliation finds a payment still processing after the cut-off, and PayGate has no charge with its reference. What does it do?
questions.explain: This is the crash between transaction 1 and the charge. Old enough and unknown to the gateway means the charge never happened. Reconciliation never charges; it only settles.
options: Marks it declined ("never reached the gateway"), so the order is free for a new payment attempt

questions.q: A client retries with the same key while its payment is still unknown. What does the service do?
questions.explain: The retry is an occasion to learn the outcome, never to charge again. That is how the "database failed after the charge" demo recovered with one charge.
options: Charges again with a new key
Looks the charge up at the gateway by reference, settles it if found, and returns the current state

questions.q: PayGate answers 402 card_declined. How does the adapter treat it?
questions.explain: Retries are for failures that may pass (5xx, timeouts). A decline is the gateway's decision about this card.
options: As a final answer: declined. It is not retried, because the same card will be declined again

questions.q: PayGate answers 401 bad_key. Why does the adapter throw instead of returning an outcome?
questions.explain: Mapping it to "declined" would tell customers their cards are bad while every payment fails because of us.
options: Because 401 means the customer must log in
A wrong API key is our configuration bug: no customer action helps, and it must become a logged 500 that alerts someone

questions.q: Two simultaneous requests with the same key: the test accepts 409 or a replay for the loser, but exactly one fresh 201 and one charge. Why not require exactly 201 and 409?
questions.explain: Test the invariant (one charge, no second fresh success), not the schedule. Flaky tests teach people to ignore failures.
options: Because the test framework is slow
Which one happens depends on timing: the loser gets 409 while the winner runs, or the replay if it arrives after. Demanding one interleaving makes the test flaky

questions.q: What does the type argument in bus.on<Event<PaymentEvent>>("payment.succeeded", …) guarantee at runtime?
questions.explain: The lesson accepts it because only settle writes these events. When other code can publish, validate the payload with a schema in the handler.
options: That the payload is validated against PaymentEvent
Nothing: it is a promise to the compiler; @zudojs/events does not check that published payloads match
That only the outbox may publish the event

questions.q: Why does Oja's API accept a card token (tok_…) and never a card number?
questions.explain: Data you never hold cannot leak from your logs, database or backups.
options: The customer enters the card in the gateway's own form; Oja's servers never see card numbers, which keeps them out of most PCI DSS requirements and out of any leak
Card numbers cannot be sent as JSON

questions.q: Why must a webhook signature be checked over the raw request body, not over JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body))?
questions.explain: A signature covers bytes. Verify first on the raw text, parse afterwards.
options: Re-serializing can change the bytes (spacing, key order, number formats), and the HMAC was computed over the exact bytes sent

questions.q: The webhook header contains a timestamp that is part of the signed text, and the verifier rejects anything older than five minutes. What attack does that stop?
questions.explain: An old but genuine message still has a valid signature. Signing the timestamp and checking its age, plus remembering event ids, stops replays.
options: Replaying a genuine, captured webhook later
A timing attack on the comparison

questions.q: What should a notification job contain?
questions.explain: Queues are stored, logged and shown in dashboards. Secrets in jobs leak there.
options: The full order with the customer's card token, so the worker needs no database
Ids and the amount: small, non-secret data; the worker loads anything else it needs

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Unknown and processing are both "accepted, not settled": 202. A decline is 402 Payment Required, a final answer.

questions.q: What does this print? (It needs Node.js.)
questions.explain: SHA-256 in hex is 64 characters and deterministic. Key order changes the JSON text, so it changes the hash. Oja builds the object itself from the parsed schema, always in the same order; for client-built objects, canonicalize first, as in the idempotency lesson.

questions.q: A conditional settle over plain objects. What does this print?
questions.explain: Unknown may still be settled, so the first two calls change it. After succeeded, every later outcome is ignored and no second event is written.

questions.q: A gateway that honours idempotency keys. What does this print?
questions.explain: The same key always returns the first charge, even with another amount; a real gateway would reject the mismatch. Two keys, two charges.

questions.q: What does this print? (It needs Node.js: it starts a real server.)
questions.explain: By default POST is not in retryMethods, so the first 503 is final. Adding POST retried twice and succeeded on the third call. Do that only when the request carries an idempotency key.
options:
default: 503 calls: 1
POST retried: { id: 'ch_1' } calls: 3

default: 503 calls: 3
POST retried: { id: 'ch_1' } calls: 3

default: 503 calls: 1
POST retried: { id: 'ch_1' } calls: 1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A second job with the same deduplication key is refused with JobDuplicateError while the first exists. The handler catches it: the receipt is already queued.

questions.q: What does this print? (It needs Node.js.)
questions.explain: A hex HMAC-SHA256 has 64 characters. Changing the timestamp changes the signature, which is why it is part of the signed text. Keys under 16 bytes are refused, so an empty secret cannot sign anything.

questions.q: An outbox relay that stops at the first failure. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first drain delivered row 1 and stopped at row 2, keeping the order. The second drain continued with rows 2 and 3. Row 1 was marked, so it was not sent again.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure. In production, keep jitter on so many failed jobs do not retry in lockstep.

questions.q: Write createPayments() with pay(userId, key, request, charge). request is { orderId, card }; charge() returns an outcome object. A new (userId, key) calls charge, stores and returns { ...outcome, replayed: false }. The same user and key with the same request returns the stored outcome with replayed: true; with a different request it returns { status: 422 }. Keys are per user. Print the results below as JSON.
questions.explain: The replay returns the stored outcome without calling charge. The fingerprint catches key reuse, and the per-user scope lets user 2 use the same key independently.

questions.q: Write toOutcome(result) for a gateway call. result is { status } for an HTTP answer or { error: "timeout" | "network" }. Map 201 to succeeded, 402 to declined, 5xx and both errors to unknown, and throw new Error("gateway configuration") for any other status. Print the outcome (or the error message) for each result below.
questions.explain: Only a real answer is final. Everything that leaves the outcome open is unknown and goes to reconciliation. Our own misconfiguration is an error that must alert someone, not a decline.
questions.expected:
{"status":201} -> succeeded
{"status":402} -> declined
{"status":503} -> unknown
{"error":"timeout"} -> unknown
{"error":"network"} -> unknown
{"status":401} -> gateway configuration

questions.q: Write reconcile(payments, gatewayCharges, now, cutoffMs). For every payment with status processing or unknown created before now - cutoffMs: if the gateway has a charge for pay_<id>, set the status to that charge's status; otherwise set it to declined. Never charge. Return the number of payments changed and print the statuses.
questions.explain: Payment 1 was charged: succeeded. Payment 2 never reached the gateway: declined, so the order can be paid again. Payment 4 is too recent; its charge may still be in flight, so it waits for the next run.

questions.q: Write an idempotent notification worker handle(job) for jobs { paymentId, kind }. It skips a job whose paymentId:kind is in sent; otherwise it calls sms(text, key) with key kind-paymentId and then adds the entry to sent. The SMS provider below throws on its first call. Run the jobs, retrying a failed job once, and print the delivered keys and sent.
questions.explain: The first attempt failed and was retried; the duplicate job for payment 1 was skipped because it is recorded as sent. The provider-side key would also cover a crash between sending and recording.

questions.q: Write startPayment(payments, orderId) that enforces "one live payment per order": if the order already has a payment whose status is not declined, return { status: 409 }; otherwise push { id, orderId, status: "processing" } with the next id and return it. Print the results below.
questions.explain: After a decline the order is free again; while a payment is live, another attempt is refused. In PostgreSQL the partial unique index enforces this even when two requests race, which a check in code cannot.

questions.q: With @zudojs/schema, write NewPayment: orderId a positive integer and card a string matching /^tok_[a-z0-9_]{2,60}$/. Print safeParse results for the three bodies: the data, or the paths of the issues.
questions.explain: The client's amount is stripped, a raw card number is refused (it should never reach the server), and the order id must be a real id. The amount is then read from the order.
